fields.h1: The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life: A Guide
fields.meta_title: The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life: A Guide
fields.description: Hannah Whitall Smith’s beloved classic offers a secret to a happy Christian life: surrender and trust. A guide to the book, its themes, and how to read it.
fields.body_html:
Hannah Whitall Smith’s The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life is one of the best-loved devotional books ever written, a warm and practical classic that has led generations of believers out of anxious, defeated Christianity into rest and joy. Written by a nineteenth-century Quaker whose own faith had passed through deep struggle, it is not a book of lofty theory but of tested experience. Its promise is bold: that there is a secret to a genuinely happy Christian life, available to any believer, and that it is far simpler than we imagine. This guide unpacks that secret, walks through the book’s two great themes, and shows how to read it for yourself.

What the book is about

Smith wrote for Christians who were truly converted yet miserable — burdened, striving, and frustrated, sensing there must be more than their up-and-down experience. Her diagnosis is that many believers trust Christ for their salvation but try to live the Christian life in their own strength, and so are perpetually exhausted and discouraged. The “secret” she offers is the recovery of a life she describes, in her own words, as “the life hidden with Christ in God” — the very phrase Paul uses: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Colossians 3:3).

The happy life, in other words, is not a matter of better circumstances or stronger willpower but of a right relationship of trust with God. It is the difference between carrying our own burdens and rolling them onto God; between striving to be good and letting God make us good. Smith insists this life is not for a spiritual elite but for every ordinary believer willing to take God at his word.

The secret in two words: surrender and trust

Smith reduces the secret to two simple movements, which she calls the human side and the divine side. She states it memorably: “man’s part is to trust and God’s part is to work.” Our part is not to accomplish our own transformation but to hand ourselves over to God and rely on him to do it. Two things are asked of us — entire surrender (giving God every part of our lives) and complete trust (believing he will then do his work) — and God does the rest.

She pictures it with the image of a potter and clay: God “takes the abandoned clay and begins to work it,” molding it to his own will once it is fully yielded. Our striving actually hinders the work; our surrender releases it. This is the double heartbeat of the book — abandon yourself to God, and trust him utterly — echoing Paul’s “present yourselves to God” (Romans 6:13) and Solomon’s “Trust in the Lord with all your heart, and do not lean on your own understanding” (Proverbs 3:5).

Key themes to watch for

As you read, watch for Smith’s steady insistence on faith over feelings. She teaches that we are to rest on the fact of God’s promises, not on the fluctuations of our emotions — a lesson that has steadied countless anxious believers. Feelings will follow in time, but faith takes God at his word first, regardless of how it feels.

A second theme is casting every care on God. Smith applies the promise “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7) with wonderful practicality, showing how to actually hand over our worries rather than merely talking about it. A third is the resulting peace — “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding” (Philippians 4:7) and the promise that God “will keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on” him (Isaiah 26:3). The happy life, in Smith’s telling, is finally a peaceful one, because it has stopped trying to carry what only God can carry.

How the book is arranged

Smith divides her book into two parts, and knowing the shape helps the reader. The first part answers the question of the life itself — what this hidden life with Christ is, how it is entered, and how the doubts and difficulties that keep believers out of it can be overcome. Here she lays her foundation: the human side of surrender and the divine side of God’s working, the two movements on which everything else rests.

The second part turns to the results — the practical fruit of the surrendered, trusting life. Here Smith walks through how this life changes our attitude toward temptation, toward failure, toward guidance, toward difficulties and disappointments, showing what happens in daily experience when a believer truly commits their way to the Lord. This two-part structure — first the principle, then the practice — makes the book eminently usable: the reader is not left with a lovely idea but shown how it works out in the ordinary business of living. Throughout, her governing text might be Jesus’ own promise of rest to the heavy-laden (Matthew 11:28), for the whole book is an extended invitation to lay down the burden of self-effort.

How to read it

This is a book to be lived, not merely studied. Smith writes directly and personally, often anticipating the reader’s objections, so read it as a conversation — argue back if you must, but be honest about where your own faith falls short of her invitation. Take it slowly, a chapter at a time, and actually practise what she describes: where she urges surrender, surrender; where she urges trust, choose to trust.

Some readers find her nineteenth-century optimism needs balancing with the Bible’s realism about ongoing struggle; read her, as you would any devotional writer, with an open Bible and a discerning heart. But do not let caution rob you of her central gift, which is entirely biblical: the call to stop striving in your own strength and rest in God. Test her secret by trying it, and see whether the peace she promises is real. She would be the first to say that the proof of the book is not in admiring its argument but in living it, for the happy life is not a theory to be debated but a rest to be entered.

Why it still speaks today

More than a century on, the book endures because the problem it addresses — the weary, anxious, self-reliant Christian — is as common as ever. In an age of exhaustion and worry, Smith’s message of rest is medicine. She points tired believers away from themselves and toward the God who has promised to do the work, if only they will let him.

The book has also had a remarkable reach. Since its publication it has been translated into many languages and has never gone out of print, becoming a staple of the deeper-life tradition and shaping how countless believers understand sanctification. Part of its appeal is Smith’s plain, homely style — she illustrates her points with everyday pictures a child could grasp, and writes not as a distant teacher but as a fellow-traveller who has known the misery she describes and found the way out. Readers feel understood, and then gently led.

Its enduring power is that it takes the great doctrines of grace and makes them breathe in daily life. Justification by faith becomes sanctification by faith; the God who saved us by grace is trusted to keep and change us by grace too. That is why readers who take it to heart so often describe a genuine turning point — the moment their Christianity stopped being a burden and became a rest. Weary, anxious, self-reliant believers are as common now as in Smith’s day, perhaps more so, and to all of them her message is medicine: stop striving in your own strength, hand yourself over to God, and trust him to do the work. It is not a call to do more but to rest more — to exchange the exhausting project of self-improvement for the restful reliance of faith. “Commit your way to the Lord; trust in him, and he will act” (Psalm 37:5).

Read it for yourself

No summary can replace the book’s own warm and persuasive voice, so go to it directly and let Smith lead you, chapter by chapter, into the rest she found. Come ready not merely to admire her secret but to practise it — to surrender and to trust — and you may find, as so many have, that the happy life she describes is not beyond your reach but as near as a simple act of faith. Read it, too, alongside her companion volume of comfort for the suffering, and let both books lead you into the same rest: a life no longer carried on our own shoulders but hidden safely with Christ in God. “The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). That life of faith is the secret, and it is offered to you.
